title: Enterprise Security, Identity, Zero Trust, Privacy, Audit & Threat Detection
method: Every P28 requirement is control N of a domain, and every one carries the same acceptance criterion: it 'passes when allow/deny behavior, tenant isolation, least privilege, audit evidence, threat/failure handling, key/secret lifecycle, monitoring and mapped security tests are verified'. Eight conditions, all required. A requirement is verified only when its domain exists AND all eight conditions hold. Nothing is inferred.

acceptance_conditions.note: All eight are required. They are assessed platform-wide because security boundaries, evidence and lifecycle are platform properties.

allow/deny behavior.evidence: Deny is the default in two independent places. Row level security is ENABLEd and FORCEd on all 131 tables with explicit policies, and the anon role holds no table privilege beyond the public plan catalog — so a policy mistake alone cannot expose business data. The API gateway returns typed denials in a fixed order, and an unknown key is answered identically to a malformed one so the endpoint cannot become a key-existence oracle. 556 database tests and 65 gateway tests.

tenant isolation.evidence: app.assert_security_gates() runs at the end of every migration that adds a table and refuses to apply if any is left open, and tests/governance/registry.test.ts asserts the same independently. app.enforce_tenant_parent refuses a child row attached to a parent owned by another company, which RLS alone does not prevent for a user who belongs to two. Reporting views run security_invoker, checked at migration time and by test. Cross-tenant reads are exercised from two provisioned companies throughout.

least privilege.evidence: Roles carry explicit permission sets and approval tiers; API keys carry scopes and reach only their own company, and no scope widens that; helper functions are SECURITY INVOKER where they read tenant data and SECURITY DEFINER only with a pinned search_path; the anon role holds nothing. The gateway asserts every write route requires a write scope.

audit evidence.evidence: An append-only ledger recording prior and new state for every governed table, protected by trigger against update and delete. Library row history records what every library row used to say. The API request log records failures as well as successes, and a revoked key is retained so old requests still resolve to the key that made them.

mapped security tests.evidence: Security behavior is tested rather than asserted: 51 RLS tests, 65 gateway authorization tests, 49 redaction and observability tests, and governance tests that fail the build if a table is unclassified or a category invariant is broken. 1,740 tests in all, with the production migrations run unmodified against real PostgreSQL 18.

threat/failure handling.gap: Failure handling is strong and tested: the gateway never throws to a caller, a failed connector run is a row rather than an exception, engines refuse invalid input, and prompt injection from retrieved documents is treated as untrusted input by contract. Threat handling does not exist. There is no threat detection, no anomaly detection, no security alerting, no incident response procedure and no written threat model. The controls name the threats they answer in comments, which is not a model anyone can review.

key/secret lifecycle.gap: The holding is sound: secrets live in server-side environment variables and never reach the browser, connector credentials are stored as handles into a secret store rather than values, and API keys are stored only as a SHA-256 hash with a display prefix, are scoped, expirable and revocable. The lifecycle is absent: nothing rotates a key, no expiry policy is enforced, there is no certificate inventory, no vault integration, and no record of when a secret last changed.

monitoring.gap: General observability now exists — structured logging with correlation, metrics, and health and readiness endpoints. Security monitoring does not. No security metric is defined, nothing counts failed authorizations or privilege changes, nothing establishes a baseline, and nothing alerts. The signals are being produced and nobody is listening to them.

partial.Data Minimization: Some by construction: the API returns named columns rather than rows wholesale, and logs are redacted. Nothing states what may be collected or for how long.
partial.Encryption at Rest: Supabase encrypts storage and the database at rest. The platform neither configures nor evidences it, so the control is inherited rather than owned, and nothing here would notice if it changed.
partial.Encryption in Transit: Traffic is HTTPS by deployment. Same as at rest: inherited, not owned or evidenced.
partial.Identity Governance: Memberships, invitations and roles exist with an owner flag and approval tiers. There is no joiner/mover/leaver lifecycle: nothing drives access from an employment change, and nothing reviews it afterwards.
partial.Privacy Controls: Raw card data is never stored — Stripe holds it and only a brand and last four reach this platform. Beyond payment there is no privacy control: no consent record, no subject access path, no export or erasure.
partial.Privileged Access: Approval tiers and an owner flag gate consequential actions, and self-approval is refused. There is no just-in-time elevation, no time-bounded grant, and no separate review of what privileged accounts did.
partial.Secrets Management: Secrets live in server-side environment variables and never reach the browser, connector credentials are held as handles into a secret store rather than values, and API keys are stored only as a SHA-256 hash. What is missing is lifecycle: no rotation, no expiry policy, no vault integration, no record of when a secret was last changed.
partial.Security Metrics: The metrics engine exists and the API emits request and latency metrics. No security metric is defined — nothing counts failed authorizations, privilege changes or anomalous access.
partial.Session Security: Supabase issues and validates sessions. This platform sets no session policy of its own — no inactivity bound it enforces, no step-up for a privileged action, no way to revoke one session rather than all.
partial.Zero Trust: Several of the properties hold in practice — every request is authorized on its own, nothing is trusted by network position, and the anon role holds no table privilege. It is not stated or verified as a model, so it is a set of habits rather than an architecture anyone can audit.

not_built.Access Reviews: No periodic review of who holds what.
not_built.Anomaly Detection: Nothing establishes a baseline or notices departure from it.
not_built.Attack Surface Management: No inventory of exposed surface and no monitoring of it.
not_built.Attribute-Based Access: Access is role and membership based. There is no attribute policy — nothing decides on project, region, classification or time of day.
not_built.Backup Security: No backup configuration owned by this platform. P31.
not_built.Certificate Management: No certificate inventory, expiry monitoring or renewal.
not_built.Compliance Evidence: No control mapping to any framework and no evidence collection.
not_built.Container Security: No container build or hardening. P31.
not_built.Data Classification: No classification exists. Every column is treated alike, so nothing can be handled according to its sensitivity.
not_built.Dependency Security: No dependency scanning or advisory monitoring. The engine and PDF packages have zero runtime dependencies, which shrinks the surface but is not a program.
not_built.Event Security: There is no event bus, so there is nothing to secure. Dependent on the Domain Events gap named in P24.
not_built.Forensic Evidence: The audit ledger and API request log would serve as evidence, but nothing preserves, exports or chains custody of it.
not_built.Incident Response: No runbook, no severity model, no containment procedure.
not_built.Infrastructure Security: No infrastructure as code and no infrastructure controls. P31.
not_built.Key Management: No key management. Nothing rotates, escrows or records the lifecycle of a key.
not_built.MFA: Not implemented. The company settings screen previously displayed a 'Require multi-factor authentication' toggle that nothing enforced; it has been removed and MFA is now named as unavailable. The capability itself remains absent.
not_built.Network Security: No network policy, segmentation or egress control. Belongs to P31 infrastructure, which is separately unverified.
not_built.Policy Attestation: No policies to attest to and no attestation record.
not_built.Retention & Deletion: No retention policy, no scheduled deletion, no legal hold. The settings screen displays 'Retention: Indefinite', which is a description rather than a control.
not_built.Runtime Security: No runtime protection or workload hardening. P31.
not_built.SAST/DAST: No static or dynamic security analysis in the pipeline.
not_built.SCIM Provisioning: No SCIM endpoint. Membership is managed in the application only.
not_built.SSO Federation: No SAML or OIDC federation. Every user authenticates directly.
not_built.Security Administration: No security administration surface — no console for policy, keys, sessions or reviews.
not_built.Security Alerting: Nothing alerts. Structured logs and metrics now exist, but nothing consumes them.
not_built.Security Exceptions: No exception register, so a knowingly accepted risk has nowhere to live.
not_built.Threat Modeling: No threat model is written down. Individual controls name the threat they answer in comments, which is not the same as a model anyone can review.
not_built.Vulnerability Management: No scanning, triage or remediation tracking.

notable_finding.subject: MFA toggle with nothing behind it
notable_finding.finding: apps/web/src/pages/app/settings.tsx rendered a 'Require multi-factor authentication' toggle, and no code read or enforced it. Three further toggles in the same panel had the same problem — enforce single sign-on, session timeout after 12 hours, restrict exports to administrators — none of which had a backing column or any reader. The same screen displayed 'Retention: Indefinite' as though it were a policy.
notable_finding.why_it_matters: An absent control is a gap somebody can plan around. A control the interface says is on, that nothing implements, is a false assurance — an administrator who enables it believes their organization is protected. This is the only place in the platform where the interface claims a security property the code does not have.
notable_finding.disposition: Recorded here and carried into the P28 not_built entry for MFA. Either the toggle is implemented or it is removed; leaving it is the one option that should not stand.
notable_finding.resolution: All four toggles removed. The security panel now lists the eight controls the platform actually enforces, each naming the mechanism that enforces it so a claim can be checked rather than taken on trust, and a separate 'Not yet available' card names multi-factor authentication, single sign-on, session policy, export restriction and retention as absent. The audit tile reads 'No policy set' instead of 'Indefinite'. apps/web/src/pages/app/settings.test.tsx asserts the security panel renders no switch at all — not merely no MFA switch, because a narrower test would let the next unbacked toggle through — and that every claimed control names its mechanism. 6 tests.
